{{Short description|Concept in contact topology}}

In the [[knot theory|mathematical theory of knots]], the '''rotation number''' is an invariant associated with knots that are adapted to a contact structure, such as [[Legendrian knot|Legendrian]] and [[transverse knot|transverse knots]], in a three-dimensional [[contact geometry|contact manifold]]. It measures the twisting of the knot's tangent direction relative to the contact structure. Together for the [[Thurston–Bennequin number]] for Legendrian knots, it is often referred to as a "classical" invariant of Legendrian knots.

The rotation number of a knot <math>K</math> is commonly denoted by <math>\operatorname{rot}(K)</math> or <math>r(K)</math>.

==Definition and properties for Legendrian knots==
Let <math>K</math> be a null-homologous oriented Legendrian knot in a co-oriented contact three-manifold <math>(M,\xi)</math> and fix a Seifert surface <math>\Sigma</math> for <math>K</math>, that is an embedded connected, compact, orientable surface with boundary <math>\partial \Sigma = K</math>. The rotation number <math>\operatorname{rot}(K,\Sigma)\in \mathbb{Z}</math> of <math>K</math> relative to <math>\Sigma</math> is defined as the [[winding number]] of a positive tangent vector field to <math>K</math> with respect to a trivialization of <math>\xi</math> over <math>\Sigma</math>.<ref>{{cite book
|title= An introduction to contact topology; Volume 109 of Cambridge studies in advanced mathematics
|last=Geiges 
|first=Hansjörg
|authorlink=Hansjörg Geiges 
|year=2008 
|publisher=Cambridge University Press 
|location= 
|isbn=978-0-521-86585-2 
|page=94 
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RERR4zMDYRgC&dq=%22Legendrian+knot%22&pg=PA94 }}</ref>
This definition can be extended to Legendrian knots with other topological types.

One shows that <math>\operatorname{rot}(K,\Sigma)</math> only depends on the class <math>[\Sigma]\in H^2(M,K)</math> associated with the surface <math>\Sigma</math>. Moreover, whenever the Euler class <math>e(\xi)</math> of the contact structure vanishes, the rotation number is independent of the above choice and is hence denoted <math>rot(K)</math>. The rotation number is invariant under Legendrian isotopy.

=== The Euclidean case ===
We consider the case where <math>(M,\xi)=(\mathbb{R}^3,\xi_{\mathrm{std}})</math> is [[Contact geometry#The standard contact structure|the standard contact structure]] on <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math>.

A theorem due to Eliashberg-Fraser<ref>{{cite book
 | last1 = Eliashberg
 | first1 = Yakov
 | last2 = Fraser
 | first2 = Michael
 | chapter = Classification of topologically trivial Legendrian knots
 | title = Geometry, Topology and Dynamics
 | series = CRM Proceedings & Lecture Notes
 | volume = 15
 | publisher = American Mathematical Society
 | year = 1998
 | pages = 17–51
}}</ref> asserts that two Legendrian knots that are topologically the unknot in <math>(\mathbb{R}^3,\xi_{\mathrm{std}})</math> are Legendrian isotopic if and only if their classical invariants agree. Note that this classification theorem does not hold for general topological types.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Chekanov
 | first = Yuri
 | title = Differential algebra of Legendrian links
 | journal = Inventiones Mathematicae
 | volume = 150
 | year = 2002
 | issue = 3
 | pages = 441–483
 | doi = 10.1007/s002220200212
| bibcode = 2002InMat.150..441C
 }}</ref>

====Front projection description====
The rotation number of a Legendrian knot <math>K</math> can be computed combinatorially from the front projection. It is given by

:<math>
\operatorname{rot}(K)=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\#\text{downward cusps}-\#\text{upward cusps}\bigr),
</math>

where cusps are counted with respect to the orientation of the knot.
====Lagrangian projection description====
The rotation number of a knot in <math>(\mathbb{R}^3,\xi_{\mathrm{std}})</math>  is related to the classical notion of [[rotation number]] as follows. Let <math>i\colon S^1\to \mathbb{R}^3</math> be a parametrization of a knot <math>K</math>.
Then

:<math>
\operatorname{rot}(K)=\operatorname{rot}(\pi_L\circ i),
</math>

where <math>\pi_L\colon \mathbb{R}^3\to \mathbb{R}^2</math> is the standard Lagrangian projection to the first two coordinates.
